subject: music
title: Punk (c. 1974–1978): short songs, small rooms, a fight with the 1970s
dek: After the long songs and large rooms of the early 1970s, New York and London — overlapping years, different class politics — brought the track back to two minutes. Independent labels, fanzines, and a few small clubs did the work. The press called it punk.

thumb.alt: White canvas awning over a Bowery doorway, red gothic letters reading CBGB and OMFUG, with the number 315 on both sides.

hero.alt: The white awning of CBGB at 315 Bowery, red letters CBGB and OMFUG, brick walls, a recessed door, and a green fire hydrant on the sidewalk.
hero.caption: CBGB, 315 Bowery, photographed on 1 October 2005, while the club was still open. The letters on the awning are the original joke: Country, Bluegrass, Blues. Hilly Kristal opened the room in December 1973. The T-shirts in the window and the later posters are 2005. The address is the 1970s fact.
hero.credit: Adam Di Carlo / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 3.0

honesty: “Punk” is a press and fan word, not a union card. New York and London made short, loud records in overlapping years. They were not copies of each other, and they did not share a committee. Cleveland, Akron, Brisbane, Sydney, and late-1970s Tokyo were contemporaneous rooms, not a required pairing. MC5, the Stooges, and the New York Dolls are precursors — loud, short, ugly records before the word stuck. This lesson stops at the first wave. Post-punk and hardcore are named as the next rooms, not taught. 1970s band photographs are usually still in copyright, so the pictures here are venue exteriors and one museum object, all later than 1978 and captioned as such. Where a free picture could not be found, the lesson does without. No AI people.

timeline.label: Rooms and precursors
timeline.detail: Hilly Kristal opens CBGB at 315 Bowery, 10 December 1973. The New York Dolls have already issued a debut (1973). In London, Malcolm McLaren and Vivienne Westwood restyle 430 King’s Road as SEX in 1974. Pub rock is filling British pubs with short R&B. These are feeders and precursors, not yet the word “punk.”

timeline.label: Horses / first Pistols gig
timeline.detail: Patti Smith’s Horses (Arista, 10 November). The Ramones are a CBGB regular. The Sex Pistols play their first gig at Saint Martin’s School of Art, 6 November. New York’s fiscal crisis is a fact of the streets around the Bowery; Britain is in recession.

timeline.label: Records, fanzines, Grundy
timeline.detail: Ramones (Sire, 23 April). The Saints issue “(I’m) Stranded” on Fatal Records in Brisbane (September). Mark Perry starts Sniffin’ Glue (July). The 100 Club Punk Special, Oxford Street, 20–21 September. The Damned’s “New Rose” (Stiff, 22 October). “Anarchy in the U.K.” (EMI, 26 November). Bill Grundy’s Today interview, Thames Television, 1 December.

timeline.label: Majors, bans, Bollocks
timeline.detail: EMI drops the Sex Pistols in January; A&M signs and drops them in one week in March; Virgin signs in May. “God Save the Queen” (27 May). The Clash (CBS, 8 April). Television’s Marquee Moon (February). X-Ray Spex, “Oh Bondage Up Yours!” (September). Never Mind the Bollocks, Here’s the Sex Pistols (Virgin, 28 October) enters the UK Albums Chart at number one. Wire’s Pink Flag (December).

timeline.label: The first wave burns out
timeline.detail: Sex Pistols’ last gig of the original run: Winterland, San Francisco, 14 January 1978. The group splits. Nancy Spungen dies in October 1978; Sid Vicious dies in February 1979. Tokyo Rockers gigs at S-KEN in Roppongi from July 1978. Post-punk and hardcore are already opening other rooms. They are the after, not this lesson.

fun_fact.title: The album went to number one while a shop was in court for the sleeve
fun_fact.text: Virgin released Never Mind the Bollocks, Here’s the Sex Pistols in the United Kingdom on 28 October 1977. On the Official Albums Chart dated 12 November it entered at number one, and it held the top place the following week. While it sat there, police in Nottingham charged the manager of Virgin’s local shop under the Indecent Advertisements Act 1889 for displaying the sleeve in the window. Richard Branson hired the barrister John Mortimer. On 24 November 1977, Nottingham magistrates acquitted the manager. The court was told that “bollocks” could mean nonsense. The record stayed in the shops. The useful fact is the overlap: a number-one LP and a Victorian indecency statute in the same fortnight, and the statute lost.

sections.title: Stadiums, solos, and a hangover from the 1960s

blocks.text: The psychedelia years had left rock with longer songs, larger crowds, and a business that billed the LP as the work. By the early 1970s that habit had hardened. Stadium rock sold a night in a football ground. Guitar solos ran past the length of a 1964 single. Progressive rock treated a side of an album as a suite. Glam put the costume back on the television. None of that was a crime. It was a job, and it paid. It was also what a younger crowd in small rooms would refuse: the distance from the stage, the time on the clock, the idea that musicianship meant more notes. The British Invasion had been a 45 rpm export. Ten years later the same industry was selling duration.

The refusal had economics under it, not only taste. Britain in the mid-1970s was in recession. Unemployment, especially among the young, was a newspaper fact, not a lyricist’s metaphor. The International Monetary Fund loan of 1976 is the official marker; the dole queue was the local one. New York City’s fiscal crisis in 1975 put the Bowery and the rest of a nearly bankrupt city in the same shot: empty lots, a city government bargaining with Washington, a downtown that landlords had not yet renamed. People who write about punk like to make those facts a soundtrack. Treat them as weather. The records came from rooms that were cheap because the neighbourhoods were cheap.

Britain already had a feeder that was not stadium rock. Pub rock, in the first half of the 1970s, put short rhythm-and-blues back into rooms that held a few hundred people. Dr. Feelgood, from Canvey Island, were the usual example: guitar, a suit, a set that did not wander. Joe Strummer’s 101ers were another. The point was a small stage and a song that ended. Pub rock did not call itself punk. It trained players and audiences for a shorter night, and some of those people — Strummer among them — walked into the next rooms when those rooms opened.

A few older American records had already been loud, short, and ugly. The MC5’s Kick Out the Jams (1969) was a live Detroit album that did not behave like a studio photograph. The Stooges, with Iggy Pop, issued The Stooges the same year and Raw Power in 1973. The New York Dolls’ debut (1973) was glam from the wrong side of the river: makeup, riffs, songs that did not last. Later writers filed all three as “punk.” In 1969–73 they were not a movement with that name. They were precursors. The useful fact is the method — volume, brevity, a refusal of polish — sitting on the shelf before CBGB’s awning meant anything to a weekly paper.

sections.title: Two cities, overlapping years, different class politics

blocks.text: Do not start with London copying New York, or New York copying London. The years overlap. The class politics do not. In New York the room that mattered was a Bowery bar whose owner had wanted country, bluegrass, and blues. In London the headquarters was a clothes shop on the King’s Road, and the explosion was a live television interview. Both cities made two-minute songs. They were not one scene with two addresses.

Hilly Kristal opened CBGB on 10 December 1973 at 315 Bowery, in a part of Manhattan that the city’s 1975 fiscal crisis did not spare. The letters stood for Country, Bluegrass, Blues. What he got, once Television’s Tom Verlaine and Richard Lloyd talked their way onto the stage with original songs, was a circuit. The Ramones, four men from Queens in leather jackets, played the room as a method: barre chords, downstrokes, no guitar solo, a set you could time with a kitchen clock. Patti Smith, already a poet, made Horses with Lenny Kaye and a band, produced by John Cale, and issued it on Arista on 10 November 1975. Blondie — Debbie Harry and Chris Stein — and Talking Heads used the same small stage for pop and art-school nervousness that the later word “new wave” would try to separate. Richard Hell left Television, wrote “Blank Generation,” and took the ripped shirt onto a New York stage before London made a fashion of it. Johnny Thunders, out of the New York Dolls, formed the Heartbreakers and later took that band to London. Max’s Kansas City, on Park Avenue South, booked overlapping bills. The New York fact is a few rooms, a few dozen people, and records that Sire and Arista were willing to tape. It is not a proletarian uprising. Many of the players had art-school or poetry credentials. The Bowery supplied the rent, not a manifesto.

blocks.alt: The stained white CBGB & OMFUG awning with red letters and the number 315, hung indoors over a doorway beneath a red EXIT sign.
blocks.caption: The CBGB awning, photographed in 2014 at the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in Cleveland. The fabric is dirty and torn at the edge. The EXIT sign is the museum’s, not the club’s. This is an object: canvas, paint, and a Bowery address, not a 1976 performance shot.

blocks.text: London’s 1976 was a different argument. Malcolm McLaren had already been around the New York Dolls as a would-be manager. With Vivienne Westwood he ran a shop at 430 King’s Road that, from 1974, traded as SEX: fetish clothing, T-shirts that were meant to offend, clothes as a fight with hippie costume and with Carnaby Street leftovers. The Sex Pistols — John Lydon billed as Johnny Rotten, Steve Jones, Paul Cook, Glen Matlock — formed out of that counter. Their first gig was 6 November 1975 at Saint Martin’s School of Art. They were a band. They were also a media object almost immediately. EMI signed them. “Anarchy in the U.K.” appeared as a 45 on 26 November 1976. Five days later, on 1 December, they went on Thames Television’s Today programme as last-minute replacements for Queen. Bill Grundy goaded them; Steve Jones swore; the tabloids the next morning had a story they could print. The Daily Mirror’s “The Filth and the Fury” is the headline everyone remembers. The Anarchy tour that December lost most of its dates. Grundy was suspended. The Pistols were a national name before they had an album. That is not a New York story. It is a British television and newspaper story, riding a year of unemployment and an IMF loan, in which a working-class (and art-school) noise became a moral panic in a week.

blocks.alt: A narrow black-painted shop on a wet London street, with a large circular World’s End clock above a small-paned window, Chelsea terraces on either side.
blocks.caption: 430 King’s Road, Chelsea, 1 June 2010. The backward World’s End clock belongs to the shop’s identity from 1980. In 1974–76 this address was SEX, run by Vivienne Westwood and Malcolm McLaren; in December 1976 it became Seditionaries. The picture is a later facade. The number on the door is the 1976 fact.

blocks.text: The 100 Club, at 100 Oxford Street, was already a jazz basement when it became a punk address. On 20 and 21 September 1976, the 100 Club Punk Special — booked with Malcolm McLaren and the promoter Ron Watts — put the Sex Pistols, the Clash, the Damned, Buzzcocks, and Siouxsie and the Banshees (their first public set) on a two-night bill. A thrown glass during the Damned’s set blinded a young woman in one eye. Sid Vicious, not yet the Pistols’ bass player, was arrested. Violence at these shows was a real injury, not a romance, and it gave councils and venue owners a reason to cancel. The same autumn, Mark Perry’s Sniffin’ Glue, started in July 1976, showed how a scene could print itself: felt-tip, photocopy, a fanzine that told you which pub to go to. DIY here is not a slogan. It is a stapler and a shop that would take twenty copies.

blocks.alt: A red 100 CLUB light-box and matching red awning over a dark doorway on Oxford Street, with Century House and the number 100 cut into dark stone.
blocks.caption: The 100 Club, 100 Oxford Street, 22 July 2009. The trumpet on the sign is a jazz leftover; the club opened in 1942. On 20–21 September 1976 this basement held the Punk Special. The doorway in the photograph is later paint and a later calendar. The address is why it is here.

sections.title: Short songs, small labels, and three ways to be in the fight

blocks.text: A gallery of three faces is the wrong picture. Name the field, then slow down. The Ramones, Television, Patti Smith, Blondie, Talking Heads, Richard Hell, the Heartbreakers, Poison Ivy and the Cramps. In London and Manchester: the Sex Pistols, the Clash, the Damned, Buzzcocks, Siouxsie and the Banshees, X-Ray Spex and Poly Styrene, the Slits, Wire. McLaren and Westwood. Hilly Kristal. Mark Perry. Seymour Stein at Sire. Stiff Records. Geoff Travis at Rough Trade, a shop in 1976 and a label from 1978. Women were not a subplot: Smith, Harry, Siouxsie, Poly Styrene, the Slits, Poison Ivy. Clothes were an argument — Westwood’s bondage trousers, Hell’s ripped shirt, safety pins as hardware — not a Halloween costume. Independent labels made 45s when the majors were late or frightened. Violence at gigs was a booking problem. Wire’s Pink Flag, in December 1977, is already the edge of post-punk: short songs, but the next room’s grammar. That is a crowd on purpose.

The Ramones are a method. The debut album, recorded with Craig Leon at Plaza Sound and released by Sire on 23 April 1976, holds fourteen songs in about twenty-nine minutes. Johnny Ramone played barre chords with downstrokes and did not take a solo. Joey Ramone sang as if the words were a count-in. Dee Dee Ramone wrote a lot of the songs; Tommy Ramone kept time and produced in the early stretch. “Blitzkrieg Bop” is two minutes and a chant. The leather jackets were a uniform, which is a method too: you could copy it without a conservatory. What you could not fake without playing it was the speed. Later bands treated that as a rulebook. In 1976 it was four people in a Bowery bar refusing the long solo as a job.

The Sex Pistols are a media event as much as a band. The records exist, and they are short: “Anarchy in the U.K.,” “God Save the Queen,” “Pretty Vacant,” “Holidays in the Sun,” then Never Mind the Bollocks in October 1977. The career around them is a sequence of institutions losing their nerve. EMI signed and, after Grundy, dropped them in January 1977. A&M signed them in March and dropped them in a week. Virgin, Richard Branson’s label, took the contract in May. “God Save the Queen” came out in Jubilee week; the BBC did not playlist it; it still sold. Sid Vicious replaced Matlock on bass in early 1977 and could barely play; he was, by then, part of the picture the papers wanted. Jamie Reid’s ransom-note graphics did the same job the clothes did: a fight you could photocopy. Listen to the album. Then read the cuttings. Neither is a footnote to the other.

The Clash are the political argument inside punk, not the only politics and not a pure one. Joe Strummer came from the 101ers. Mick Jones and Paul Simonon had been around the early London groups that never quite existed. They signed to CBS, a major, and spent a lot of “Complete Control” complaining about it. The debut album, The Clash, appeared in the United Kingdom on 8 April 1977. “White Riot,” the first single, was written after the 1976 Notting Hill Carnival clashes: white British punks watching Black Londoners fight the police and wanting a riot of their own. That is an awkward sentence on purpose. The band were more interested in reggae, in the dole, and in the idea that a three-minute song could name an enemy, than the Pistols were. They were also a rock group with a CBS catalogue number. Treat the politics as a real quarrel inside the scene — Strummer’s slogans against Rotten’s refusal — and not as a halo.

blocks.alt: A Notting Hill shopfront with a white sign reading ROUGH TRADE in black stencil letters, records in the window, a passer-by with a stroller on the pavement.
blocks.caption: Rough Trade on Talbot Road, 30 April 2009. Geoff Travis opened the first Rough Trade shop in Notting Hill in 1976 and the label in 1978. This is a later West London storefront, not a 1976 photograph. The stencil on the fascia is the independent-label fact made into a sign.

blocks.text: The rest of the field is not a supporting cast. The Damned got the first UK punk 45 out: “New Rose,” Stiff Records, 22 October 1976, a week before “Anarchy.” Buzzcocks, from Manchester, treated the short song as pop — Pete Shelley and, at the start, Howard Devoto — and by September 1978 were on Top of the Pops. Television’s Marquee Moon (February 1977) is a CBGB record that allows a guitar to run, which is why it sits awkwardly in any list that thinks punk only means two chords. Wire, from London, made Pink Flag at the end of 1977: twenty-one tracks, most of them brief, already looking at the next room. Poly Styrene of X-Ray Spex shouted “Oh Bondage Up Yours!” in 1977 as a refusal of the same 1970s, from a different mouth. The Slits formed in 1976; their first album is 1979, which is why this lesson names the band and not the LP. Poison Ivy, with the Cramps, took rockabilly and a New York stage and did not ask permission. Patti Smith’s Horses remains the New York document that is a book as well as a record. Name them because they were there, not because a syllabus needed a balance.

sections.title: The same years, not a ranking of cities

blocks.text: In Brisbane, the Saints recorded “(I’m) Stranded” in 1976 and issued it themselves on Fatal Records in September, with Ed Kuepper and Chris Bailey, because no Australian major wanted it. Copies went to British music papers. Sounds called it single of the week. EMI in London signed them. The 45 is earlier than “New Rose” and “Anarchy.” That is a date, not a trophy. Brisbane under Joh Bjelke-Petersen was a police town; the Saints were not a King’s Road boutique band, and they did not take kindly to being told to look like one when they reached England in 1977. In Sydney, Radio Birdman were playing a related short, loud set, closer to the Stooges than to McLaren, and issued Radios Appear in 1977. Australia was not waiting to be notified.

In Cleveland and Akron, a Midwestern circuit had been making difficult records before the British tabloids discovered the word. Rocket from the Tombs lasted long enough in 1974–75 to split into Pere Ubu and the Dead Boys. The Dead Boys went to CBGB. Pere Ubu stayed stranger. Devo, from Akron, were art-school Ohio in the same years; Q: Are We Not Men? A: We Are Devo! is 1978. None of this is London exported to the lakes. It is a set of American rooms that used some of the same older records — Stooges, Velvets — and did not need a Grundy interview to exist.

In Japan, the calendar runs a little later, which is why it belongs here as contemporaneous and not as a twin. SS formed in Kyoto in 1977 with the stated aim of playing faster than the Ramones; their records came out after the fact. In Tokyo, from July 1978, the musician and promoter S-KEN ran Sunday gigs at his Roppongi studio under the name Tokyo Rockers — Friction, Lizard, Mirrors among them — and Shinjuku Loft, which had opened in October 1976, was one of the live rooms. A live compilation followed in 1979. That is the end-edge of this lesson’s years, a local circuit hearing imported 45s and answering in Japanese rooms. It is not an assigned Asian verse to make the map look fair.

sections.title: 1978–79: the first wave ends, other rooms open

blocks.text: The Sex Pistols’ last concert of the original run was at the Winterland Ballroom in San Francisco on 14 January 1978, a Bill Graham room, far larger than CBGB or the 100 Club. Sid Vicious was barely playing. Lydon ended the night with a question — “Ever get the feeling you’ve been cheated?” — and left. The group split. Nancy Spungen died in New York in October 1978. Vicious died in February 1979. Those dates are the burnout of one band and one press story, not a moral. By then the first-wave rooms were already emptying or turning over. What opened next were other rooms with other names: post-punk, which kept the shortness and changed the harmony and the rhythm; and hardcore, which kept the shortness and raised the speed. Wire were already on that hinge. This lesson does not teach those eras. It only notes that 1974–78 was a fight with the 1970s, and that the fight did not end when the Pistols did. It moved.
If a two-minute song in a small room is a refusal of stadiums and solos, who still owns that refusal once the tabloids, the majors, and the uniform arrive?

glossary.explain: Press and fan word, mid-to-late 1970s, for short, loud guitar music associated with a few small clubs, independent 45s, and a fight with stadium rock. Not a single committee or sound.

Club at 315 Bowery, New York, opened 10 December 1973 by Hilly Kristal. The letters meant Country, Bluegrass, Blues. The room that booked the Ramones, Television, Patti Smith, Blondie, and Talking Heads.
The rest of CBGB’s awning joke: Other Music for Uplifting Gormandizers. Printed under CBGB on the canopy.
A homemade magazine, usually photocopied. In this lesson, Mark Perry’s Sniffin’ Glue (from July 1976) is the London example: which bands, which pubs, written by a participant.
British early-to-mid-1970s circuit of short rhythm-and-blues in pubs, associated with Dr. Feelgood and groups such as the 101ers. A feeder for some London punk players, not the same movement.
Here, making and distributing records, fanzines, and clothes without waiting for a major label or a glossy magazine. A stapler, a shop, an independent 45 — not a brand.
Bill Grundy, presenter of Thames Television’s Today. On 1 December 1976 he interviewed the Sex Pistols live; Steve Jones swore; the next day’s papers made the band a national story.
A record company outside the major groups, or acting like one. Sire, Stiff, Rough Trade, and Brisbane’s Fatal are the examples in this lesson. Majors (EMI, CBS, Virgin) also signed punk acts.
Mid-1970s rock billed for sports arenas and long shows. One of the things first-wave punk was refusing: distance from the stage and time on the clock.
Early-1970s rock that put costume and makeup on television. The New York Dolls came from its messy side. London punk fought the costume as well as using it.
Early-to-mid-1970s album rock that treated a side of an LP as a suite. Part of the furniture punk shortened.
The mid-to-late 1960s stretch of studios, ballrooms, and longer songs. The hangover this lesson is fighting. See the earlier capsule.
American press name, from 1964, for British beat groups on the U.S. charts. A 45 rpm industry. Ten years later the same business was selling duration. See the earlier capsule.
Guitar chords made by laying one finger across a fret. Johnny Ramone’s method, with downstrokes and no solo.
Picking only in one direction. Part of the Ramones’ guitar method; it makes a fast song sound even and hard.
The rooms that opened as the first wave burned out: still short, but with different rhythm and harmony. Named here as an after, not taught. Wire’s Pink Flag sits on the hinge.
A later, faster punk that kept the shortness and raised the speed. Named here as a next room, not taught.
Later radio and press name that tried to separate pop and art-school groups (Blondie, Talking Heads) from the word “punk.” In 1976 they were on the same CBGB bills.
Owner of CBGB. Opened the club on 10 December 1973 wanting country, bluegrass, and blues; booked original bands instead.
Partner with Vivienne Westwood in the King’s Road shop; manager of the Sex Pistols. Had already circled the New York Dolls. Clothes, press, and a band as one project.
Designer. With McLaren ran 430 King’s Road as SEX (1974–76), then Seditionaries. Bondage trousers and offensive T-shirts as an argument, not a souvenir.
McLaren and Westwood’s shop at 430 King’s Road, 1974–76. Fetish clothing and T-shirts. The London headquarters before it was a chart story.
The same 430 King’s Road shop from December 1976, after SEX. Later still World’s End (from 1980), whose backward clock is in the photograph.
Name of the 430 King’s Road shop from 1980, with a backward clock. Later than this lesson. The photograph is this facade; the 1976 fact is the address.
Chelsea street address of SEX / Seditionaries / World’s End. London punk’s clothes shop, not its only venue.
Music basement at 100 Oxford Street, London, open since 1942 (as a jazz club). Hosted the Punk Special, 20–21 September 1976.
Two-night bill at the 100 Club, 20–21 September 1976. Sex Pistols, Clash, Damned, Buzzcocks, Siouxsie and the Banshees’ first public set. A thrown glass blinded a young woman in one eye.
Booker at the 100 Club who helped put on the Punk Special with McLaren.
New York club-restaurant on Park Avenue South. Overlapping bills with CBGB in the mid-1970s.

San Francisco promoter. Winterland was his room. In this lesson he is that date, not the Fillmore’s 1960s story.

Television singer and guitarist. Helped talk Kristal into original bands at CBGB.
Television guitarist.
New York poet and singer. Horses (Arista, 10 November 1975), with Lenny Kaye, produced by John Cale. A CBGB-era document that is also a book.
Patti Smith Group guitarist. Compiled the Nuggets garage anthology; played on Horses.
Produced Horses. Former Velvet Underground; in this lesson he is that desk, not a 1967 ballroom story.
CBGB group around Debbie Harry and Chris Stein. Pop on the same small stage. Later called new wave; in 1976 it was the same room.
Blondie singer.
Blondie guitarist.
CBGB group. Art-school nervousness on the same bills as the Ramones. Later radio called it new wave.
Singer of Siouxsie and the Banshees. In the Pistols’ Grundy entourage; first Banshees set at the 100 Club Punk Special.
London group. First public set at the 100 Club Punk Special, 20 September 1976, with Sid Vicious on drums that night.
London group. Pink Flag (December 1977): twenty-one short tracks, already the edge of post-punk.
Singer of X-Ray Spex. “Oh Bondage Up Yours!” (1977). A different mouth in the same fight with the 1970s.
London group, Poly Styrene. Virgin single “Oh Bondage Up Yours!” September 1977.
London group, formed 1976. Named here as a band in the scene; their album Cut is 1979, after this lesson’s window.
Guitarist of the Cramps. New York, 1976, with Lux Interior. Rockabilly on a punk stage.
Poison Ivy and Lux Interior. Formed in New York in 1976. Contemporaneous, not a London franchise.
Singer of the Cramps.
Detroit group. Kick Out the Jams (1969). A loud, short precursor, not yet “punk” as a 1970s press word.
Iggy Pop’s Detroit group. The Stooges (1969); Raw Power (1973). Precursor records, not a 1976 club.
Stooges singer. Named here as a precursor, not as a 1977 Berlin chapter.
New York group, debut 1973. Makeup and short riffs. Precursor; McLaren circled them. Johnny Thunders came from here.
Canvey Island pub-rock group. Short R&B in pubs in the first half of the 1970s. A feeder, not punk.
Joe Strummer’s pub-rock group before the Clash.
Brisbane group, Chris Bailey and Ed Kuepper. “(I’m) Stranded,” Fatal Records, September 1976. A date before the first UK punk 45s, not a trophy.
Saints singer.
Saints guitarist and co-writer of “(I’m) Stranded.”
Sydney group. Short, loud, closer to the Stooges than to McLaren. Radios Appear, 1977.
Cleveland group, 1974–75. Split toward Pere Ubu and the Dead Boys.
Cleveland group after Rocket from the Tombs. Stayed stranger; did not need to move to the Bowery to exist.
Cleveland group that went to CBGB. One American Midwest line into the New York room.
Akron group. Art-school Ohio in the same years. Q: Are We Not Men? A: We Are Devo! is 1978. Contemporaneous, not a London copy.
Kyoto group, formed 1977, aiming to play faster than the Ramones. Records issued later. Contemporaneous Japan, not a twin of CBGB.
Name of Sunday gigs at S-KEN’s Roppongi studio from July 1978, and of the bands around them (Friction, Lizard, Mirrors). End-edge of this lesson’s years.
Tokyo musician and promoter. Ran the 1978 Roppongi studio gigs billed as Tokyo Rockers.
Tokyo group in the Tokyo Rockers circle, from 1978.
Tokyo live room, opened 1 October 1976 in Nishi-Shinjuku. One of the rooms for the late-1970s Tokyo circuit.
Artist for Sex Pistols sleeves and posters. Ransom-note lettering as graphics you could photocopy.
Barrister who defended the Nottingham Virgin shop manager over the Bollocks sleeve, November 1977.
British group. Cancelled a Today appearance on 1 December 1976; the Sex Pistols replaced them. In this lesson they are that gap, not a discography.
Died in New York, October 1978. Named as a date in the first wave’s burnout, not as a symbol to decorate a paragraph.
Queensland premier in the Saints’ Brisbane years. A police-state local fact, not a British tabloid.
London carnival. Clashes with police in August 1976 were the prompt Strummer cited for “White Riot.”
The 1976 British loan is the official marker of a fiscal crisis. Unemployment was the local one.
New York City’s 1975 near-bankruptcy. Weather for the Bowery rents, not a lyric.
The Ramones’ debut album, Sire, 23 April 1976. Fourteen tracks, about twenty-nine minutes. The method on disc.
Opening track and single from Ramones, 1976. About two minutes. Official Rhino/Warner audio exists.
Patti Smith album, Arista, 10 November 1975. Produced by John Cale. A New York document before the 1976 45s.
Opening track of Horses. Smith’s verses into Van Morrison’s “Gloria.” The Horses album version is the listen here, not a later demo.
Sex Pistols’ first single, EMI, 26 November 1976. Later on Never Mind the Bollocks. Five days before the Grundy interview.
Sex Pistols single, Virgin, 27 May 1977, Jubilee week. The BBC did not playlist it. It sold anyway.
Sex Pistols single, 1977, on Never Mind the Bollocks.
Sex Pistols single, 1977, on Never Mind the Bollocks.

glossary.term: Never Mind the Bollocks, Here’s the Sex Pistols
aliases: Never Mind the Bollocks Here's the Sex Pistols
glossary.explain: Sex Pistols album, Virgin, 28 October 1977. UK number one on the chart dated 12 November. The sleeve put a Nottingham shop in court; the manager was acquitted on 24 November.
Victorian statute used against the Bollocks sleeve in a shop window. Nottingham magistrates acquitted, 24 November 1977.
Daily Mirror headline after the Grundy interview, December 1976. A tabloid fact, not a documentary title in this lesson.
The Clash’s debut album, CBS, UK 8 April 1977. (The group of the same name is also in this glossary.)
Clash single, CBS, 18 March 1977. After the 1976 Notting Hill Carnival clashes. Official video on theclashVEVO.
Clash single about, among other things, their CBS contract. A political argument that includes the label.
Damned single, Stiff, 22 October 1976. First UK punk 45, a week before “Anarchy in the U.K.”
Television album, February 1977. CBGB band, long guitar lines. Official recordings exist; this lesson does not pirate a fan upload.
Richard Hell song and 1977 Voidoids album. A New York phrase and a ripped shirt.
X-Ray Spex single, Virgin, September 1977. Poly Styrene. Official Universal/Castle audio exists.
Wire album, December 1977. Twenty-one short tracks. The hinge toward post-punk, not a post-punk syllabus.
Saints single, Fatal Records, Brisbane, September 1976. Self-issued; then EMI in London. A date, not a world-championship.
Radio Birdman album, 1977, Sydney.
MC5 live album, 1969. Precursor volume, not a 1976 fanzine.
Stooges debut album, 1969. Precursor.
Stooges album, 1973. Precursor.

glossary.term: Q: Are We Not Men? A: We Are Devo!
glossary.explain: Devo album, 1978. Akron contemporaneous, not a CBGB franchise.

glossary.term: Ever Fallen in Love (With Someone You Shouldn’t’ve?)
aliases: Ever Fallen in Love (With Someone You Shouldn't've?)
glossary.explain: Buzzcocks single, 1978. The listen here is the Top of the Pops performance of 21 September 1978, official Domino/BBC upload, not the studio 45.
BBC chart television. Buzzcocks appeared 21 September 1978. A first-wave group on an official pop show at the end of this lesson’s years.
West London. Rough Trade’s first shop was here; the Carnival clashes of 1976 sit in the Clash story. Same district, different jobs.
Australian city. Home of the Saints. Not a suburb of Oxford Street.
Australian city. Home of Radio Birdman.
Ohio city. Rocket from the Tombs, Pere Ubu, Dead Boys. A Midwest circuit in the same years.
Ohio city. Devo. Contemporaneous art-school Ohio, not a formula pairing.
Japanese city. SS formed here in 1977.
Tokyo district. S-KEN’s studio and the 1978 Tokyo Rockers Sundays.
Essex. Home of Dr. Feelgood. Pub rock’s usual example.
New York borough. The Ramones came from here to the Bowery.
Soho boutique strip of the 1960s. Named here as the leftover London look SEX was fighting, not as another Invasion chapter.
British tabloid. “The Filth and the Fury” was its headline after the Grundy interview.
British music weekly. Called the Saints’ “(I’m) Stranded” single of the week in 1976.
Tokyo group in the 1978 Tokyo Rockers circle.
Tokyo group in the 1978 Tokyo Rockers circle.
